analysis.one_liner: Caps the all-in cost of consumer credit at 36 percent, covering payday loans, overdraft fees, and credit cards.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would cap consumer credit costs at 36 percent and cover fees, never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a national 36 percent ceiling into law for the total cost of consumer credit — counting interest plus fees, late charges, overdraft fees, and add-on products together. It would have applied to payday loans (which average about 400 percent a year), car title loans (about 300 percent), bank overdraft fees (which can run far higher), and credit cards. Loans made above the cap would be unenforceable, lenders would face criminal penalties, and state attorneys general could sue violators.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who currently pay triple-digit rates and heavy fees — payday and car title borrowers, bank customers hit with overdraft fees, and cardholders paying high credit card rates — would keep the money they now pay in fees and interest. The bill's own findings put overdraft fees alone at roughly $14 billion a year, payday loans at about $7 billion, and car title loans at about $3.8 billion [S3]. Borrowers who took an illegal loan could void the debt and get their payments back [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bars any creditor from making a consumer loan whose combined interest and fees exceed 36 percent, counting late fees, overdraft and over-limit fees, credit insurance premiums, and add-on products in the calculation [S2] [S3].

Makes loans above the cap unenforceable: the lender cannot collect the debt in court or arbitration and must return principal, interest, charges, and fees, and borrowers can raise the violation as a defense at any time [S3].

Adds criminal penalties — up to one year in prison and a fine of the greater of three times the accrued debt or $50,000 per violation — and lets state attorneys general sue violators in federal court [S2] [S3].
Replaces the standard APR disclosure on credit card statements with an all-in 'FAIR' rate so cardholders see the true cost including fees [S2] [S3].
Applies to every form of consumer credit with no exemptions — the bill forbids regulators from waiving the cap — and lets states keep stricter rules of their own [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, car title lenders, high-cost online installment lenders, and banks that collect overdraft and high credit card interest would lose the revenue above the cap — revenue the bill itself estimates in the tens of billions of dollars a year [S3]. Some borrowers with poor credit could also lose access to small-dollar credit entirely, since lenders who can no longer charge rates that cover their risk may stop serving them.

drawbacks.text: A 36 percent cap priced out of high-risk borrowers' reach means some low-income consumers who use payday loans today may have nowhere to turn for emergency cash; lenders who cannot price for the risk often stop lending to that population rather than lend at a loss [S3].

Because the cap counts all fees together, banks could no longer collect most overdraft and late fees or charge subprime cardholders rates that reflect their default risk, which could mean fewer credit cards and less generous terms for weaker borrowers [S3].
Loans made in violation would be voided and lenders criminally prosecuted, a remedy some argue could chill lending to borderline borrowers even where the loan would have been repaid [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the households currently paying 400 percent payday rates or repeated overdraft fees, the savings are large and immediate — the bill estimates $14 billion a year on overdrafts alone [S3]. The real cost is access: borrowers with the worst credit may lose a legal source of emergency cash, and the bill offers no funded replacement like postal or public small-dollar lending. The military experience the bill cites — a 36 percent cap on loans to servicemembers since 2006 that curbed payday lending around bases — is the strongest evidence the tradeoff can work [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee took no action on it — no hearing, no vote — and it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Durbin introduced the bill on July 27, 2017, joined by five other Democratic senators as original cosponsors [S1] [S3] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, where the action record ends [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday and car title lenders, high-cost online installment lenders, and banks collecting overdraft and high card fees kept their revenue — the bill was never even scheduled for a committee vote.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Merkley, Whitehouse, Blumenthal, Gillibrand, and Franken
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the bill never gained any cosponsors beyond the original six Democrats.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.role: Chairman, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill received no action after referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: High-cost lending industry
against.role: Payday, car title, and installment lenders
against.what_they_did: Opposed a 36 percent national rate cap, which would eliminate the bulk of their revenue; the bill was referred to the Banking Committee and never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run Senate Banking Committee never acted on the bill [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The cap would outlaw rates averaging about 400 percent a year, wiping out most payday lending revenue — about $7 billion a year by the bill's estimate [S3]. The industry's business depends on charging rates far above the cap.

Banks collect roughly $14 billion a year on overdraft loans, which can exceed 17,000 percent on an annualized basis, plus high card interest; the bill counts overdraft and late fees toward the cap [S3]. Card issuers would also have to disclose an all-in FAIR rate.
Three-hundred-percent-average car title loans would be void above the cap, eliminating about $3.8 billion in annual fees [S3].
Online installment loans charging triple-digit rates — unreported revenue by the bill's estimate — would be capped, and no regulator could exempt them [S3].
